question: What do experts agree on where evidence is thin?

nasa2021.cite: Nasa, Jain & Juneja (2021). Delphi methodology in healthcare research: How to decide its appropriateness. World Journal of Methodology 11(4): 116 ff.
nasa2021.checked: every quote read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC8299905) on 20 Nov 2026; the full text has no page numbers, so places are section headings; in-text reference numbers are left out of the quotes; the last page was not checked

steps.title: Choose the panel
steps.text: Decide in advance who counts as an expert for this question, then invite people who meet those criteria.

quotes.text: The panel member selection is undoubtedly the most crucial aspect of Delphi research studies
The selection of a panel or voting members in a Delphi study should be based on objective and predefined criteria and related to the problem under study.

steps.title: Rate anonymously
steps.text: Each expert rates every statement alone, usually on a numbered scale. Nobody knows who gave which rating, so no one can dominate.

quotes.text: The anonymity of individual members in a Delphi study removes the inherent bias like dominance and group conformity (defined as groupthink) observed with face-to-face group meetings.

steps.title: Feed back
steps.text: After each round, send everyone the group's results (median, spread, anonymous comments) and let them reconsider.

quotes.text: After each of the survey rounds, obtained data are analyzed and presented in an easily interpretable format to all the panel experts.
Controlled feedback gives insight to the individual member about the trend and one can change its response if needed.

steps.title: Repeat the rounds
steps.text: Rate again, round after round. Consensus is judged by a rule fixed beforehand, such as a share of experts agreeing.

quotes.text: The consensus definition used commonly is the percentage of agreement based on a predefined cut-off, central tendency, or a combination of both. However, percentage agreement varies widely from 50%-97% and is selected arbitrarily

steps.title: Stop when stable
steps.text: Stop when the answers no longer change from one round to the next, by a stopping rule written down before the first round.

quotes.text: Stability is defined as the consistency of responses between successive rounds of a study
The criteria for stopping the Delphi rounds based on consensus or stability should be identified a priori.

exercise.title: Watch the rounds converge
exercise.intro: Fifteen experts rate one statement from 1 (disagree) to 9 (agree). Each row is a round; the green line is the median that everyone sees before the next round. Run rounds until the answers settle.

quote.text: consensus can be there in unstable responses, and stability can be there without consensus

exercise.data_label: Example data, made up for this exercise.
exercise.model_note: The simulated experts: in each round 20% keep their rating; the others move between 30% and 80% of the way towards the median, rounded to a whole number. Stable means the share rating 7–9 changed by 5 points or less and the interquartile range did not change.

limits: The card's reference, Dalkey & Helmer (1963), was not read; the page follows Nasa et al. (2021), a review of how Delphi studies are run and judged in healthcare. The ACCORD reporting guideline (Gattrell et al. 2024) was found but not read.
The exercise's experts follow a made-up rule; real panels can also drift apart, drop out, or move away from the median.
The step texts in our own words are summaries of the quotes beside them; the quotes are the authority.
